opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think caregiving is one of the most important things human beings do, and also one of the most neglected, both in science and in our broader thinking about society. If you look at the developmental work I've done for many years, the thing that's really striking about human beings is that we have this incredibly long childhood. We have a much longer period of immaturity than any other species, and that only works if there are people who are willing to take care of those helpless, demanding creatures for a really long time.

So in a sense, the flip side of thinking about children and how they learn is thinking about the people who make that learning possible. Mothers, of course, but also fathers, grandparents, alloparents, all the people who invest in children. And caregiving isn't just about children. We take care of the elderly, the sick, people who are vulnerable in all sorts of ways.

What's interesting is that caregiving doesn't fit very well into the standard models we have, whether that's economic models or political philosophy. Those tend to assume autonomous agents making deals with each other, exchanging goods, pursuing their own interests. But caregiving is a relationship where one person puts enormous resources into another person with no expectation of return, and the goal is to make that other person more autonomous, to let them go off and do things the caregiver might not have anticipated or even approve of. That's a deeply puzzling thing from the perspective of a lot of our theories, and yet it's absolutely fundamental to how human beings have evolved and how our cultures work. So I think it deserves a lot more scientific attention than it's gotten.

r001.rationale: The response describes caregiving as involving resources and no expectation of return, but does not say it is unpaid work or that GDP does not account for it.

r002.rationale: It says caregivers invest resources so recipients can become more autonomous and pursue things the caregiver may not anticipate or approve of.

r003.rationale: The response mentions caring for the elderly, but does not raise how elders help care for other people.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think caregiving is one of the great puzzles that we've neglected, both in philosophy and in cognitive science and in economics, for that matter. If you look at the history of philosophy, the picture of the human being is somebody who's autonomous, who's rational, who's making decisions for themselves, who's thinking about their own preferences. And of course, the thing about caring for someone, especially caring for a child, is that it doesn't fit into that picture at all. You're taking a being who doesn't have your preferences, who's going to become something you can't predict, and you're putting enormous amounts of resources into that being without any expectation that you're going to get something back in return.

And the striking thing from an evolutionary perspective is that this isn't some sort of side issue for human beings. Humans have this very long period of childhood, much longer than any other primate, much longer than any other animal, and that's connected to the fact that we have these great big brains and that we learn so much. But you can't have a creature that spends twenty years learning without having someone to take care of it while it's learning. So we've got this combination: we have grandmothers, we have fathers, we have what the anthropologists call alloparents, the whole village that's involved in taking care of children. And that caregiving is what makes our distinctively human intelligence possible in the first place.

So when I started looking at how children learn, which is what I've been doing for most of my career, it became clearer and clearer that you couldn't understand the learner without understanding the people who are making the learning possible. And then the other thing that struck me is that the kind of intelligence you need to be a caregiver is itself very interesting and very different from the kind of intelligence we usually celebrate. You have to be able to attend to another creature, figure out what they need, change what you're doing as they change, and let them become autonomous rather than controlling them. That seems to me to be a profound kind of intelligence, and we really don't have a good theory of it. We don't even really have a good language for it. We tend to think of it as something that just comes naturally, especially to women, and so it's invisible. And I think that's a mistake, both scientifically and, frankly, morally.

r001.rationale: The response says caregiving is neglected and involves substantial resources, but does not mention unpaid care or GDP accounting.

r002.rationale: It describes investing resources in a child and letting the child become autonomous, but does not characterize this as advancing the recipient’s own goals.

r003.rationale: It mentions grandmothers among those involved in caring for children, but does not explain how elders help care for others.

astra-6.text:
I think caregiving is one of the most extraordinary things that human beings do, and it’s been remarkably neglected in philosophy and psychology. We spend a lot of time thinking about how individuals make decisions or pursue their goals, and much less time thinking about how we make it possible for another person to develop goals of their own.

That’s particularly striking when you think about children. They have this long period when they can explore and learn without having to worry about getting dinner on the table. But that freedom is possible because somebody else is getting dinner on the table. You can’t understand the intelligence of children without understanding the care that supports it.

And there’s a fascinating tension there. You’re deeply committed to this person, but the point isn’t to produce a particular outcome that you’ve specified in advance. It’s to enable someone to become a person who may be quite different from you, who may want things you never anticipated. I think that deserves a much more central place in our account of what it means to be human.

r002.rationale: It says caregiving makes it possible for another person to develop goals of their own and provides the support that lets children explore and learn.

r003.rationale: The response discusses children and caregiving generally, but does not raise how elders help care for others.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’ve spent most of my career thinking about how children learn, and that leads naturally to a question about the people who look after them. Children can explore and experiment because somebody else is making sure that they’re safe and fed and loved. So caregiving isn’t just something that happens in the background. It’s part of what makes our extraordinary capacity for learning possible.

And there’s a broader puzzle here. We tend to describe human intelligence in terms of what an individual can accomplish. But we spend an unusually long time dependent on other people, and then we devote an enormous amount of effort to caring for others. I think that relationship between being able to explore and being cared for is central to understanding what makes us human.
